curator_prompt:
These are mistakes and lessons from a diagnostic agent's attempts on 60 different patients.
The agent asks questions, orders tests under a budget, then commits to one diagnosis.
Write a playbook of at most 10 short, general rules (each at most 200 characters) that would have
prevented the most frequent and costly mistakes. Rules must apply across diseases: do not name any
specific disease, syndrome, organism or gene. Order them by how often the mistake occurred.
Return {"rules": ["...", "..."]}.
rules: Treat a diagnosis as provisional until decisive evidence is available; appearance, risk factors, and suggestive imaging rarely establish a specific cause alone.
Use only documented findings: a planned, ordered, or repeated test is not a result, and an unanswered question is not a positive finding.
Do not anchor on one symptom, prior diagnosis, or isolated test. Reconcile the whole presentation and investigate clues that do not fit your leading explanation.
When a lesion or abnormality remains uncertain, choose the test that best localizes or characterizes it; obtain tissue confirmation when appropriate before naming its cause or subtype.
Do not stop at a syndrome or complication when important findings remain unexplained; pursue the underlying cause or source.
Choose tests and questions for a specific decision they can change. Avoid repeating completed studies or spending turns on low-yield, undocumented history.
Act promptly on red flags and progressive symptoms: prioritize the targeted imaging or evaluation needed to rule out dangerous, time-sensitive causes.
